reason: This is the one I expected to break and it survived. My prior was that Frick's sentence opens 'Founding libraries was like constructing more public granaries', which is how the line usually circulates, and that 'The founding of libraries' would be a later smoothing. I was wrong. I downloaded the scan the verifier names and searched it. The string 'granar' occurs twice in the whole book, and the second occurrence reads: 'The beauty of the gulfs bore fruit with the opening of harbours. The founding of libraries was like constructing more public granaries, amassing reserves against a spiritual winter which by certain signs, in spite of myself, I see ahead. I have done much rebuilding.' So the definite article is Frick's own and the quotation is verbatim up to the cut. Edition confirmed from the scan's own front matter, which reads MEMOIRS OF HADRIAN BY MARGUERITE YOURCENAR, Translated from the French by Grace Frick in Collaboration with the Author, LONDON SECKER AND WARBURG. Section confirmed structurally, not by trusting the verifier: the heading TELLUS STABILITA stands at character 270198 of the flattened text, SAECULUM AUREUM at 374078, and the passage at 330574, so it falls inside Tellus Stabilita. Page confirmed by the running heads, which in this scan sit at the top of each page (page 10's head is followed by text continuing a sentence broken from page 9): the head carrying 134 precedes the passage and the head carrying 135 follows it, so page 134 is right, and the printed contents put Saeculum Aureum at 161, which is consistent. The note is honest and necessary, since the full stop is a cut and Frick's sentence runs on; the cut lands on a grammatically complete clause. Translator and year are right, Frick's translation having first appeared in 1954. shipped.js: not shipped, no near match, Yourcenar at zero of three, not banned. Format: source line is 95 characters, leads with the name, no dash, no straight double quote, and the speaker parenthetical precedes the translation parenthetical as the rule prescribes. Naming Hadrian is correct, since the novel is his first-person memoir. Scope clean: novel, French 1951 and Frick's English 1954, publishable, Fiction is the form. Weakest leg is theme fit, since this is aphoristic reflection rather than counsel, but the month's blurb admits maxims and aphorisms. I did not add a page to the source line because the printing is not named there and a bare page number would travel badly.
